records.our_prose: Newly emerged spring leaves are thickened, puckered, curled, and flushed red to purple. This is peach leaf curl, caused by the fungus Taphrina deformans, which infects the young leaves as buds swell in cool, wet spring weather. Growers often reach for a spray once they see it, but no spray cures curled leaves; the infection is already complete. The only effective control is a dormant fungicide applied on the leafless tree, so the real action belongs to next dormancy, not this spring. Keep the tree watered and fed to carry it through the season.

records.our_prose: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill the hole with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.
